record.card: Woodworking makes useful or decorative objects from wood through crafts such as carving, turning, and joinery. Material choice influences the process. Exploring grain and workability reveals why different woods respond differently to cutting, gluing, and finishing.

evidence.note: Supports craft examples, grain, workability, tools, adhesives and finishes.

record.card: Woodworking includes carving, turning, and joining wood into useful or decorative objects. Choosing a shape also means working with a changing material: wood gains and loses moisture. Drying and design can reduce the dimensional changes that otherwise affect a finished piece.

evidence.locator: Lead, line 172; Factors in choosing materials, lines 305–307
evidence.note: The lead identifies woodworking practices, including carving, turning and joinery.

evidence.locator: Drying Stresses, pp. 13–7 to 13–8; introductory moisture-control discussion p. 13–1
evidence.note: Introductory discussion explains moisture changes and how drying and design limit subsequent dimensional problems.

imported_records.description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.
imported_records.subsection: Crafts & making

record.label: Woodworking
record.learning_takeaway: Connect shaping and joining wood with the need to accommodate wood’s moisture-driven movement.
record.original_description: Shaping and joining wood to create practical or decorative objects.

relations.note: Editorial making bridge: grain-dependent movement and moisture changes help explain why material choice and joinery must accommodate dimensional change.

evidence.note: The report discusses responsive justice services and identifies cost, time, complexity, geographical distance, legal capability and language as access barriers.

record.card: John Rawls’s 1971 book A Theory of Justice develops justice as fairness. Its hypothetical choice of social principles removes knowledge of personal advantages behind a veil of ignorance. Without knowing their eventual position, the choosers cannot tailor institutions simply to favor their own class or talents.

evidence.locator: §1 Life and Work; §4.6 The Original Position
evidence.note: Identifies the 1971 book and explains the informational restrictions preventing arbitrary advantage in the original position.

record.label: A Theory of Justice
record.learning_takeaway: See why Rawls deprives hypothetical choosers of knowledge of social advantages when selecting principles.

relations.note: The book offers an account of just social institutions by using hypothetical agreement, a concrete project in political philosophy.

record.card: An actuarially fair insurance premium equals expected claims for the relevant risk group. It is a pricing benchmark, not a judgment about social fairness. A real insurer also needs to cover operating expenses and, where applicable, profit, so an actual premium can exceed expected payouts.

evidence.locator: Risk Groups and Actuarial Fairness; How Insurance Works
evidence.note: Expected-loss benchmark and the stated claims/expenses/profit accounting support the distinction.

record.label: Actuarially fair insurance
record.learning_takeaway: Separate an expected-claims premium from one that also covers expenses and profit.

relations.note: The source defines actuarial fairness as a benchmark for insurance premiums using expected claims in a risk group.

record.card: Antidiuretic hormone changes kidney water handling by moving aquaporins, or water-channel proteins, into collecting-tubule cell membranes. More water can then leave the forming urine and return to the bloodstream. When the signal declines, channel removal reduces this permeability again.

evidence.note: The ADH section and Figure 26.12 describe insertion/removal of water channels and resulting changes in collecting-tubule permeability and water recovery.

record.label: ADH-dependent aquaporin trafficking
record.learning_takeaway: Explain reversible insertion of water channels into collecting-tubule membranes as a way to conserve body water.

relations.note: Editorial feedback classification: regulated water-channel insertion alters renal water loss, helping oppose changes in blood-plasma concentration.

record.card: Adverse selection can occur when buyers privately know their risk better than insurers. A premium based on average risk may discourage safer buyers, leaving a costlier pool. Further price increases can worsen that sorting, even without anyone changing their behavior after buying coverage.

evidence.note: Private risk information and the departing low-risk buyers example support the selection spiral.

record.label: Adverse selection
record.learning_takeaway: Trace how privately known risk changes who chooses to buy coverage.

relations.note: Privately known characteristics alter which exchanges occur; this economic sorting mechanism differs from changes in behavior once a contract exists.

record.card: The regular English plural has different spoken endings in cats, dogs, and buses, yet each adds the same plural meaning. These are allomorphs: alternative forms of one morpheme, a small meaning-bearing unit. Comparing them separates variation in pronunciation from a change in grammatical function.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; a/an and plural suffix examples
evidence.note: One plural morpheme has three spoken realizations with stable meaning.

record.label: Allomorph
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize different forms that express one morpheme, including spoken plural variants.

relations.note: Allomorphs are alternative forms of meaning-bearing morphemes, making them units investigated in word-structure analysis.

record.card: An allophone is one pronunciation variant within a phoneme, the sound category a language treats as a unit. English speakers can produce voiced and devoiced versions of l without changing a word’s identity. Many such variants are predictable from nearby sounds; others vary more freely.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: noncontrastive variants and distribution
evidence.note: Noncontrastive l variants; conditioned distribution and free variation.

record.label: Allophone
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish noncontrastive pronunciations of one phoneme from meaning-changing sound contrasts.

relations.note: Phonology investigates how a language organizes noncontrastive sound variants and their environments.
An allophone is a realization grouped within a phoneme; the distinction separates concrete variants from the sound category.

record.card: Analepsis takes a narrative back to events earlier than its current position. In the Aeneid, books two and three recount happenings that precede book one. Separating the order of telling from the order of events shows how a flashback rearranges a story without changing its chronology.

evidence.note: Flashback definition and Aeneid books 2–3 example.

record.label: Analepsis
record.learning_takeaway: Track a return to earlier events relative to a story’s current narrative position.

relations.note: Tracking analepsis is a specific method for analyzing how literary narration reorganizes event order.

record.card: Wood does not shrink equally in every direction. Drying generally changes dimensions most around growth rings, less across them, and very little along the grain. Combined with curved ring patterns, these unequal movements can turn an initially regular board into a distorted piece.

evidence.locator: Fiber Saturation, pp. 4–2 to 4–3; Dimensional Stability, p. 4–7
evidence.note: The dimensional-stability section orders tangential, radial and longitudinal shrinkage and explains shape distortion from unequal movement and curved rings.

record.label: Anisotropic shrinkage of wood
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why a board changes shape as drying shrinkage differs around growth rings, across rings, and along the grain.

relations.note: Directional differences in wood shrinkage follow growth-ring and grain orientation and explain distortion during drying.

record.card: Aquatint creates areas of printed tone using a grain of acid-resistant material on a metal plate. Acid bites between the protected particles, producing a textured surface. Different depths yield different tonal effects, while ordinary line etching often supplies outlines that the tonal process does not provide.

evidence.note: Granular resist, acid-biting depth, tone and combination with line etching.

record.label: Aquatint
record.learning_takeaway: Create tonal areas through a granular acid-resistant ground instead of relying on drawn outlines.

relations.note: Aquatint adapts acid biting to a granular ground so an etched plate holds tonal areas rather than just linear marks.

record.card: The Archimedes Palimpsest is a medieval Greek prayer book made from reused parchment. Earlier writing was scraped away, and leaves were turned and folded again. Beneath the prayers survive mathematical texts, including Archimedes’ otherwise lost Method of Mechanical Theorems, showing how material reuse can preserve knowledge.

evidence.locator: The Book’s Contents; How Was it Made?
evidence.note: Reused parchment, rotated leaves, prayer text and surviving Method.

record.label: Archimedes Palimpsest
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how reuse of parchment preserved older mathematical texts underneath a prayer book.

relations.note: Because this manuscript preserves an otherwise lost Archimedean treatise, it offers a material case for studying how historians recover ancient mathematics.

record.card: In an artesian aquifer, groundwater is confined under pressure beneath relatively impermeable layers. A well lets the water rise above the aquifer’s top. It flows onto the land only when the pressure-supported water level stands above the wellhead; great depth alone is insufficient.

evidence.locator: Artesian Water; Example of an aquifer system, lines 47–61
evidence.note: The confined-aquifer discussion distinguishes rising water from flowing wells and explains the wellhead-level condition; depth alone does not define artesian water.

record.label: Artesian aquifer
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why confined groundwater rises in a well but only sometimes flows out at ground level.

relations.note: Editorial hydrology placement: the aquifer’s confinement and hydraulic pressure determine how high water rises in a connected well.

record.card: The attentional blink is a brief difficulty detecting a second target after identifying a first one in a rapid visual stream. In the original letter experiment, detection fell during a window beginning 180 milliseconds after the target. Ignoring the first target removed that pattern.

evidence.note: Reports the rapid serial letter task, onset of the impaired interval, and absence when first-target identification is not required.

record.label: Attentional blink
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a temporary second-target reporting deficit from literal blinking.

relations.note: The paper manipulates allocation of visual attention between rapidly presented targets and measures the resulting detection deficit.

record.card: Some sheet steels gain strength during an automotive paint bake. Dissolved carbon moves to dislocations created by stamping and pins them, making further deformation harder. Because this bake-hardening increase occurs after forming, the sheet can be easier to shape before becoming more dent-resistant.

evidence.locator: BH Grades, carbon pinning and post-stamping strengthening
evidence.note: Mechanism and timing apply to bake-hardenable sheet grades.

record.label: Bake hardening of steel
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how paint-bake heating lets dissolved carbon pin dislocations after steel stamping.

relations.note: Bake hardening changes selected steel grades after stamping by carbon pinning of dislocations, increasing the formed sheet’s yield strength.

record.card: Bass is a common name shared by freshwater and marine fishes, rather than one biological family. Largemouth and smallmouth bass belong to the sunfish family, while striped bass belongs to the temperate bass family. Common names can therefore hide substantial differences in classification.

evidence.note: Lead and Common types establish a shared fish name across freshwater/marine species and distinguish sunfish-family black bass from temperate-family striped bass.

record.label: Bass (fish)
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize bass as a shared fish common name rather than a single species or family.

relations.note: The bass common name refers to several fish groups, including sunfishes and temperate basses, without defining one family.

record.card: Python’s bisection functions locate where an item belongs in an already sorted list. Left and right variants fall before or after equal entries. Finding that boundary is logarithmic, but inserting into the list can still take linear time because the items must shift.

evidence.note: Sorted precondition, equal-item boundaries and search-versus-insertion complexity.
Insertion near the beginning shifts other list elements.

record.label: Bisection insertion points
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish locating ordered insertion boundaries from inserting an item, including the different complexity costs.

relations.note: The documented bisection algorithm finds an insertion boundary through comparisons, distinct from the subsequent data movement needed to insert.

record.card: Blossom-end rot produces a dark, flattened patch at a tomato’s blossom end when developing fruit lacks enough calcium. The soil may still contain plenty. Fluctuating moisture, root injury, and rapid growth can disrupt delivery, so adding calcium alone need not address the cause.

evidence.note: The disorder has dark flattened fruit-end lesions; calcium shortage in fruit can result from water, root and growth conditions despite soil calcium.

record.label: Blossom-end rot
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why calcium shortage inside developing tomato fruit need not indicate calcium-poor soil.

relations.note: Editorial gardening bridge: tomato-fruit damage may reflect disrupted calcium delivery from uneven water or injured roots, shaping cultivation choices.

record.card: A nonvolatile solute lowers a liquid solvent’s vapor pressure. At the same external pressure, the solution must then become hotter before it boils. For dilute ideal solutions, this boiling-point elevation is proportional to the concentration of dissolved particles, rather than their total mass.

evidence.locator: Boiling Point Elevation, definition and particle-concentration explanation
evidence.note: Vapor-pressure mechanism and particle-based scaling.

record.label: Boiling-point elevation
record.learning_takeaway: Connect nonvolatile solute, lowered vapor pressure, and the higher temperature needed to boil at the same external pressure.

relations.note: This effect changes the boiling temperature by lowering solvent vapor pressure at fixed external pressure; it is a specific modification of boiling point.

record.card: A finesse in bridge tries to win a trick with a card below an opponent’s highest card in that suit. Leading toward an ace–queen holding can let the queen win when the missing king lies with the opponent who must play before that holding.

evidence.note: The low lead toward ace–queen succeeds against the king held by the intervening opponent.

record.label: Finesse in bridge
record.learning_takeaway: Use play order to try to win with an intermediate honor when an opponent holds a higher card.

relations.note: ACBL teaches this leading technique as part of declarer’s play of a bridge hand, specifically to win an additional trick.

record.card: At Rothamsted, the Broadbalk Wheat Experiment has compared organic manures and mineral fertilizers since 1843. An untreated strip provides a long-running contrast. Repeated harvests let researchers examine crop and soil responses across many seasons, while documented changes in management matter when interpreting that history.

evidence.locator: Objectives and Description, lines 89–98; Experiment Design
evidence.note: The archive records 1843 establishment, mineral/manure treatments, an untreated strip, repeated harvests and soil measurements across changing design periods; interpretive caution is editorial.

record.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
record.learning_takeaway: See how repeated fertilizer and manure treatments plus an untreated strip enable long-term agricultural comparisons.

relations.note: Editorial experimental application: contrasting nutrient treatments on winter wheat turns agricultural cultivation into a continuing test of crop and soil responses.

record.card: The cadential six-four uses the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of the dominant at a cadence. Its usual move to the dominant chord shows why pitch content and harmonic function need not tell the same story.

evidence.note: Identifies I6/4 before V, dominant function, and the equivalent I/fifth notation.

record.label: Cadential six-four chord
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a chord’s tonic pitch content from its dominant function at a cadence.

relations.note: This chord’s position and resolution explain a specific relationship between chord spelling and harmonic function, making harmony the broader subject.

record.card: The Cairo Genizah preserved far more than worn sacred texts. The repository in Old Cairo’s Ben-Ezra Synagogue accumulated letters, accounts, and other documents over centuries. These fragments let historians study everyday Jewish life alongside religious learning, showing how a preservation custom can leave an unusually varied archive.

evidence.locator: Cairo’s dark chamber that remains a monument to life: repository practice paragraphs
evidence.note: Ben-Ezra repository and accumulation beyond worn sacred writing.

evidence.locator: Homepage description of Cairo Geniza and document genres
evidence.note: Letters, accounts and legal documents support everyday-life research.

record.label: Cairo Genizah
record.learning_takeaway: Learn how a synagogue repository became evidence for ordinary life as well as sacred learning.

relations.note: The collection preserves writings generated by Jewish religious practice together with evidence of the communities’ everyday lives.
The letters and accounts provide a concrete case of reconstructing historical experience from surviving primary material.

record.card: A graft succeeds only if living tissues join. The cambium, a thin growth layer between wood and bark, must contact its counterpart in the partner stem. When stem diameters differ, aligning one side can matter more than centering the scion.

evidence.locator: Terms: Cambium; Fitting the stock and scion, lines 31–32 and 115–119
evidence.note: The cambium definition and fitting instructions support growth-layer contact and one-sided alignment of stems with different diameters.

record.label: Cambial alignment in grafting
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why matching growth layers rather than outside stem edges is crucial to a graft union.

relations.note: Editorial application: grafting uses the cambium’s growth capacity by bringing the rootstock and scion growth layers into contact.

record.card: A paper towel draws liquid through its pores because the liquid is attracted both to the fibers and to itself. This capillary action can move liquid upward against gravity; it depends on interactions at narrow surfaces, without requiring a pump.

evidence.note: Wicking through fibers, adhesion, cohesion and upward motion.

record.label: Capillary action
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how adhesion and cohesion together draw liquid through narrow spaces and porous materials.

relations.note: Capillary action is liquid movement governed by adhesion to a porous surface together with cohesion within the liquid.

record.card: Making a smaller-scale map requires deciding what to omit, simplify, or emphasize. Cartographic generalization must also preserve relationships: smoothing a river could detach it from a bridge or move it through a building. Clear maps therefore require contextual decisions, not just fewer points and thinner detail.

evidence.locator: What is generalization?; river/bridge example; workflow
evidence.note: Selection/simplification and contextual river, bridge and building conflicts.

record.label: Cartographic generalization
record.learning_takeaway: Reduce map detail while preserving important spatial relationships between features.

relations.note: Generalization is the cartographic process of reducing complexity for scale while preserving recognizable landscape patterns and relationships.

record.card: Crazing is a network of fine cracks in a fired ceramic glaze. A common cause is a glaze whose thermal expansion exceeds that of its clay body. Their incompatible dimensional changes create a poor fit, and cracks may appear immediately or only later.

evidence.note: Details identify a network of cracks and a glaze–body expansion mismatch with higher glaze expansion.
Details explain immediate or delayed cracking; the thermal-expansion section identifies glaze expansion greater than the body as a common cause.

record.label: Ceramic glaze crazing
record.learning_takeaway: Relate a network of glaze cracks to incompatible thermal expansion between glaze and clay body.

relations.note: A fired coating can craze when its dimensional response does not fit the clay body, making this a specific glaze-performance problem.

record.card: Chess960 varies the starting arrangement, but castling finishes with the king and rook on the usual castling squares. On the g-side, the king ends on g1 or g8 and the rook on f1 or f8. Depending on their starting squares, one piece may remain stationary.

evidence.locator: Guidelines II.1 and II.3; PDF pp.57–58
evidence.note: Randomized setup, invariant castling destinations, and king-only or rook-only movement are explicit.

record.label: Castling in Chess960
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how varied starting squares still lead to standard king and rook castling destinations.

relations.note: Chess960 preserves ordinary piece movement and checkmate while adapting castling to randomized back ranks; this is a specific variant-rule connection to chess.

record.card: For steady gas flow without heat transfer or friction, mass flow is limited when the nozzle throat becomes sonic. With throat area and upstream total pressure and temperature fixed, this choking limits throughput. Gas may still accelerate supersonically farther downstream.

evidence.locator: Mass-flow maximum, equations 10–19 and sonic throat
evidence.note: Fixed-area and fixed-total-state sonic mass-flow limit.

evidence.locator: Sonic throat and supersonic downstream expansion
evidence.note: Choking does not prohibit downstream supersonic flow.

record.label: Choked flow
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize the ideal gas-flow limit at a sonic throat for fixed upstream total conditions and area.

relations.note: Editorial aerodynamic placement: compressibility links gas density and velocity, producing a sonic mass-flow maximum for fixed total conditions.

record.card: A clique is a set of graph vertices all joined to one another. Its members need different colors, so clique size bounds the chromatic number, the minimum colors needed, from below. The bound can underestimate: even triangle-free graphs can require more than two colors.

evidence.locator: Theorem 2.5.4; Grötzsch graph in Additional Exercise 10
evidence.note: Clique lower bound and strict-bound counterexample.

record.label: Clique lower bound on chromatic number
record.learning_takeaway: Use pairwise-connected vertices to bound colors from below, while recognizing the bound need not be tight.

relations.note: The theorem constrains proper vertex colorings through pairwise adjacency; it is a specific bound within the existing graph-coloring topic.

record.card: Fresh groundwater flowing seaward helps hold coastal saltwater back. Pumping can weaken that flow and draw saline water toward freshwater wells, including upward movement from depth. The boundary is a mixing zone, so intrusion concerns both water movement and the quality of the remaining supply.

evidence.note: The Background section describes seaward freshwater flow, pumping-induced landward/upward saltwater movement and the diffuse mixing zone.

record.label: Coastal saltwater intrusion
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how reduced freshwater flow after pumping can let saline water move toward a coastal well.

relations.note: Editorial hydrology placement: changing freshwater flow alters saline-water movement and mixing near coastal wells, linking quantity with water quality.

record.card: The cochlea sorts frequencies partly by place. High-frequency sounds excite the basilar membrane near its entrance, while lower frequencies travel farther toward the apex. Hair cells at different positions therefore respond best to different frequency ranges, converting a mechanical pattern into auditory information.

evidence.note: The hearing section maps high-frequency responses near the entrance and lower-frequency responses farther along the membrane, with locally tuned hair cells.

record.label: Cochlear tonotopy
record.learning_takeaway: Relate sound frequency to the location of strongest basilar-membrane response.

relations.note: Editorial classification: the auditory sensory system encodes sound frequency partly through the position of stimulated cochlear hair cells.

record.card: Cold moist stratification exposes certain dormant seeds to cool, damp conditions before germination. It addresses internal dormancy rather than an impermeable seed coat. Required treatment periods differ greatly among species, so a refrigerator can simulate part of a seasonal cue without supplying a universal timetable.

evidence.note: The dormancy section specifies moist cooling, internal barriers, refrigerator treatment and durations that vary by species.

record.label: Cold moist seed stratification
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a cold, moist dormancy treatment from merely chilling dry stored seed.

relations.note: Editorial placement: cold moist treatment applies knowledge of internal seed dormancy to control the timing of germination.

record.card: Common-tone modulation connects different keys through a shared pitch. In a Beethoven example, C-sharp links a C-sharp major chord to an A dominant seventh chord, helping bridge F-sharp minor and D major. One held or repeated note can preserve continuity while its harmonic setting changes.

evidence.note: Defines a single-note bridge and explicitly identifies the C-sharp connection and surrounding keys.

record.label: Common-tone modulation
record.learning_takeaway: Trace a single shared pitch used as a hinge between chords belonging to different keys.

relations.note: Reinterpreting one shared pitch across chords provides a concrete harmonic method of moving between tonal centers.

record.card: Words that act together as a sentence unit form a constituent. Linguists test candidate groups by replacing them, moving them, or using them as answers to questions. Agreement among tests supports an analysis, but a genuine constituent need not pass every test in every sentence.

evidence.locator: Replacement, Movement, Clefting, and Answers to Questions; final qualification
evidence.note: Replacement, movement, question answers and test limitations.

record.label: Constituency tests
record.learning_takeaway: Combine replacement and movement evidence to test which words act as a unit.

relations.note: These diagnostics apply linguistic observation to the specific problem of inferring which words group into phrases.

record.card: A constructive vote of no confidence removes a head of government only by agreeing on a replacement. In Germany, the Bundestag must elect a successor rather than merely reject the chancellor. A majority against the incumbent therefore does not suffice without a majority for another candidate.

evidence.note: The Bundestag glossary requires agreement on a new government head and a majority-supported successor.

record.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
record.learning_takeaway: Understand replacing a head of government by agreeing on a successor in the same parliamentary procedure.

relations.note: The Bundestag describes this as a parliamentary control mechanism that replaces the chancellor through election of a successor.

record.card: A convergent–divergent nozzle narrows to a throat, then widens. Under suitable pressure conditions, gas reaches sound speed at the throat and accelerates supersonically in the widening section. In ideal steady flow, the same widening slows subsonic gas, making flow regime essential to understanding the shape.

evidence.locator: Opening design explanation and area–velocity derivation
evidence.note: Sonic throat, supersonic expansion and contrasting subsonic behavior.

record.label: Convergent–divergent nozzle
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how an appropriately operated nozzle accelerates subsonic gas to a sonic throat and then supersonically in an expanding passage.

relations.note: The nozzle uses a choked sonic throat to set mass flow and an expanding downstream section to accelerate the resulting supersonic stream.

aliases: Countercurrent gas exchange in fish gills
record.card: Opposing water and blood flows across fish gills maintain conditions for oxygen to diffuse into blood along the whole exchange surface. Even outgoing, oxygen-enriched blood meets newly arriving water from which it can absorb more oxygen.

evidence.note: Question 10 explains opposite flows and why departing oxygen-enriched blood can still absorb oxygen from newly arriving water.

record.label: Countercurrent gas exchange in fish gills
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why opposite blood and water flows maintain an oxygen-transfer gradient along gills.

relations.note: Editorial classification: countercurrent flow is a gas-exchange mechanism within fish respiration, sustaining oxygen uptake along gills.

record.card: Cranes are long-legged, long-necked birds of the family Gruidae. Unlike herons, they fly with their necks extended. Their vocal communication includes coordinated pair calls, showing how a familiar silhouette and a distinctive sound can help identify the intended bird group.

evidence.locator: Lead, lines 228–232; Calls and communication, lines 320–324
evidence.note: Lead identifies Gruidae and extended-neck flight; Calls and communication documents pair duets. The identification suggestion is editorial.

record.label: Crane (bird)
record.learning_takeaway: Identify the Gruidae bird family and its extended-neck flight and coordinated communication.

relations.note: Cranes form the bird family Gruidae; flight posture and pair calls supply concrete family-level identification cues.

record.card: A crane raises and positions loads using lifting machinery and a supporting structure, often including a boom. Its reach is part of its design: changing the boom configuration changes what it can lift. Rated capacities therefore describe specified conditions rather than unlimited lifting power.

evidence.locator: Moving with load on the hook; Multifunctional boom systems; Precise crane control
evidence.note: A crane’s hook, lifting machinery and configurable boom.
Capacity depends on specified configuration and operating radius.

record.label: Crane (lifting machine)
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize a crane as lifting machinery whose boom configuration and load placement determine its capabilities.

relations.note: Editorial mechanical-engineering placement: hoisting mechanisms and load-support geometry jointly determine a crane’s reach and capacity.

record.card: A crane’s lifting limit changes with the load’s distance from the crane and with its setup. A longer operating radius generally means a smaller allowable load. Load charts capture these combinations, so a machine’s headline tonnage does not describe every possible lift.

evidence.locator: Section 1417: Compliance with Rated Capacity, printed pp. 47–48
evidence.note: Configuration-specific load charts and reduced capacity with longer radius.

record.label: Crane lifting capacity and load radius
record.learning_takeaway: Understand why a crane’s maximum load depends on radius and configuration instead of a single headline tonnage.

relations.note: Rated capacity is a crane-specific operating envelope indexed by boom radius, length and configuration rather than a single constant load.

record.card: Many CAM plants collect carbon dioxide at night and store it as malic acid. During daylight, they release that carbon dioxide internally for sugar production while keeping leaf pores closed. Separating these steps reduces water loss; some plants can switch CAM on and off.

evidence.note: The night/day explanation covers malic-acid storage, internal daytime carbon release, closed pores, water saving, and facultative CAM switching.

record.label: Crassulacean acid metabolism
record.learning_takeaway: Explain temporal separation of nighttime carbon capture and daytime carbon use as a water-conserving photosynthetic pathway.

relations.note: CAM is a photosynthetic pathway that stores nighttime carbon uptake as acid and uses the released carbon during daylight.

record.card: A reminder loses precision when it points to too many memories. “Recall the picture” identifies a lone picture among words more effectively than one picture among many. The cue overload principle adds an important condition to retrieval: a cue should distinguish the desired memory from competitors.

evidence.note: Contrasts a single picture with multiple pictures and explains the need for a distinctive cue–target relationship.

record.label: Cue overload principle
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why a cue linked to many memories is less diagnostic of the desired one.

relations.note: Cue overload is presented as a principle governing retrieval from memory when one cue matches multiple traces.

record.card: A tree’s rings record more than its age. Dendrochronology studies annual growth patterns to date wood and reconstruct environmental variation. Wide and narrow rings reflect changing growth conditions; matching a preserved sequence to calendar years can help date archaeological remains.

evidence.locator: Dendrochronology: The Study of Tree Rings; paragraphs on annual rings and crossdating
evidence.note: Annual rings, growth conditions, calendar matching and archaeological use.

record.label: Dendrochronology
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how annual growth rings preserve both time and environmental variation.

relations.note: Calendar-dated tree rings provide chronological evidence for preserved wood at archaeological sites.

record.card: A derangement rearranges objects so none remains in its original position. Four distinct objects have 24 permutations but only nine derangements. Inclusion–exclusion counts them by subtracting arrangements with fixed positions while correcting the overlaps between those unwanted cases.

evidence.note: No-fixed-point definition and four-object count.

record.label: Derangement
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize permutations with no fixed positions and count them by correcting overlaps among fixed-position cases.

relations.note: A derangement is explicitly a permutation with no fixed point.
The source counts derangements by applying inclusion–exclusion to sets of permutations fixing specified positions.

record.card: Affixal derivation creates a new word by adding a prefix or suffix to a base. Teach becomes teacher, changing a verb into a noun. Word class need not always change, and a derived base can take further affixes, as in computer, computerize, and computerization.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: teach/teacher and category-preserving prefixes
evidence.note: Affix-based derivation, optional category change and repeated affixation.

evidence.locator: Video Script: contrast between affixation and compounding
evidence.note: Explicit boundary: affixation attaches bound morphemes, while compounding joins typically free morphemes.

record.label: Affixal derivation
record.learning_takeaway: See how affixes create new words, sometimes without changing grammatical category.

relations.note: Affixal derivation is one way to create lexical words; compounding also forms words but joins typically free morphemes instead of attaching a bound affix.
The textbook contrasts creating a new word by derivation with supplying grammatical forms through inflection.

record.card: A nonnegative decimal integer and the sum of its digits leave the same remainder when divided by nine. Each power of ten behaves like one modulo nine, so place values collapse to their digits. The familiar divisibility test follows from that remainder-preserving shortcut.

evidence.note: Powers of ten reduce to one modulo nine and preserve digit-sum remainder.

record.label: Digit-sum divisibility test for nine
record.learning_takeaway: Explain the decimal digit-sum test using powers of ten that each leave remainder one modulo nine.

relations.note: The number-theory chapter derives the decimal test through integer congruence arithmetic, not a coincidence of examples.

record.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect. It argues that the latter may sometimes be permissible when the former is not. Proportionality and other conditions matter; merely calling harm unintended does not automatically justify it.

evidence.note: The doctrine’s intended-means/foreseen-side-effect distinction and cumulative conditions are explicit.

record.label: Doctrine of double effect
record.learning_takeaway: Separate intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect while retaining proportionality constraints.

relations.note: The entry presents double effect as a principle for judging the moral permissibility of actions with good and harmful effects.

record.card: Double weave makes two layers of cloth at the same time. Separate warp systems interlace with their wefts, while patterned versions exchange which layer sits on top. The design is built into the relationship between woven layers rather than merely printed on a surface.

evidence.note: The museum defines simultaneous cloth layers and patterned positional exchange; the contrast with a printed surface is an editorial explanation of that construction.

record.label: Double weave
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how two cloth layers woven simultaneously can exchange positions to make patterns.

relations.note: Double weave interlaces two textile layers simultaneously and can swap their positions, making its patterns a particular woven construction.

record.card: A drying board’s surface initially shrinks against a wetter core, putting the surface in tension. If that shell becomes permanently stretched, later core shrinkage can reverse the stresses. The core then enters tension, sometimes cracking internally even when the outside seems intact.

evidence.locator: Drying Stresses, pp. 13–7 to 13–8; introductory moisture-control discussion p. 13–1
evidence.note: The drying-stress section follows early shell tension, permanent set, later core tension and possible internal honeycomb cracking.

record.label: Drying stress reversal in lumber
record.learning_takeaway: Trace how a drying board shifts from outer-shell tension to inner-core tension and can develop hidden cracks.

relations.note: Editorial fabrication bridge: unequal drying of a board’s shell and core can create hidden cracks that affect lumber selected for wooden objects.

record.card: A drypoint needle scratches directly into a metal plate, pushing up a ridge called a burr beside each line. That ridge holds extra ink and produces a rich, velvety mark. Because the burr wears during printing, later impressions can lose the effect that makes early ones distinctive.

evidence.note: Scratched line, ink-holding burr, velvety effect and wear.

record.label: Drypoint
record.learning_takeaway: Connect a scratched plate’s fragile burr with its characteristic velvety printed lines.

relations.note: Drypoint is an intaglio process in which scratched metal and its retained burr carry the ink.

record.card: Signaling in economics uses something observable to convey information about something harder to inspect. Employers may treat educational credentials or awards as clues to an applicant’s abilities and persistence. The signal helps shape judgment under uncertainty; possessing the credential is not identical to demonstrating every relevant skill.

evidence.locator: Labor-market example, paragraphs on credentials, awards, and references
evidence.note: The employer example identifies credentials and accolades as signals of difficult-to-observe attributes.

record.label: Signaling in economics
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how observable credentials convey information about less observable attributes.

relations.note: Observable credentials are used in market decisions when productivity is hard to observe; that information mechanism belongs within economics.

record.card: Ekphrasis uses language to describe or respond to visual art. A poem can do more than list what a painting contains: it may question the image, imagine a figure speaking, or reflect on viewing it. The artwork becomes a starting point for interpretation as well as description.

evidence.note: Visual-art response; interpretation, imagined speech and reflection beyond description.

record.label: Ekphrasis
record.learning_takeaway: See how writing can interpret or animate visual art instead of merely describing it.

relations.note: Editorial classification: this verbal literary response to visual art belongs within literature; the cited poetic examples show one form rather than an exhaustive parent field.

record.card: A memory cue works partly by matching information encoded with the original experience. A song can bring back a particular conversation because both were linked at the time. Encoding specificity explains why the effectiveness of a reminder depends on how the event was originally remembered.

evidence.note: The song/party/conversation example and overlap-with-encoding principle support the explanation.

record.label: Encoding specificity principle
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why a cue works through overlap with how an event was encoded.

relations.note: The memory chapter states this principle as an account of which retrieval cues evoke a stored experience.

Both concern encoding–retrieval compatibility. The navigation comparison separates cue–trace information overlap from matching the cognitive operations performed during study and test; it does not claim the theories are wholly independent.

record.card: In engraving, a burin cuts sharp grooves directly into a metal plate. The printmaker varies line thickness, spacing, and crossing strokes to suggest texture and shadow. A shaded form can therefore emerge from carefully organized lines rather than from a continuous painted wash.

evidence.locator: Main text: burin; Schongauer’s strokes; Cort’s swelling lines
evidence.note: Burin-cut grooves; varied strokes, crosshatching and line thickness.

record.label: Engraving (printmaking)
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how burin-cut lines and their thickness build printed tone.

relations.note: Engraving is a printmaking method that builds the image through grooves mechanically cut into a metal matrix.

record.card: Epistemic closure asks whether knowledge survives competent deduction. A qualified principle requires knowing the premise, correctly deriving a conclusion, and believing it while retaining the original knowledge. Philosophers disagree partly because accepting closure constrains how ordinary knowledge claims can be reconciled with skeptical possibilities.

evidence.locator: Introduction; §1 K and SPK; rejection by Dretske and Nozick
evidence.note: Qualified deduction/retained-knowledge conditions and the relationship to skepticism support the explanation.

record.label: Epistemic closure
record.learning_takeaway: Examine whether competent deduction from retained knowledge yields knowledge of the conclusion.

relations.note: Closure is a proposed constraint on how knowledge extends through inference, a central epistemological question.

record.card: An eruv is a Jewish legal arrangement that permits carrying within a joined domain on Shabbat. It combines a valid enclosure with shared food that unites the residents. The boundaries follow religious-law requirements rather than property ownership, making activities such as taking a stroller outside possible.

evidence.locator: Definition; valid enclosure; shared food; uses
evidence.note: Valid enclosure, shared food, domain rules and carrying/stroller example.

record.label: Eruv (carrying enclosure)
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how a valid enclosure and shared food permit carrying within a joined Shabbat domain.

relations.note: The eruv operates within Jewish Shabbat carrying rules by joining enclosed spaces and their residents into one domain.

record.card: Etching lets acid do the cutting. An artist scratches a design through an acid-resistant coating on a metal plate; acid then bites the exposed lines. Longer exposure deepens them. After the coating is removed, those incisions provide the image for an intaglio print.

evidence.note: Ground, needle exposure, acid biting, depth and intaglio printing.

record.label: Etching (printmaking)
record.learning_takeaway: Follow how acid converts lines drawn through a protective ground into printable grooves.

relations.note: Etching produces an intaglio printing matrix by chemically biting exposed areas of a coated metal plate.
Both form metal-plate incisions, but the source contrasts etching’s acid action with engraving’s direct burin cutting.

record.card: An Euler trail crosses every edge of a graph exactly once. A finite connected undirected graph has such a trail precisely when zero or two vertices have odd degree. With two odd vertices, they must be the route’s endpoints.

evidence.locator: Section Preview; Conditions for Euler Trails
evidence.note: Edge-once definition, connectedness convention, parity criterion and endpoints.

record.label: Euler trail
record.learning_takeaway: Explain the even-degree or two-odd-degree criterion for traversing every edge of a connected finite undirected graph exactly once.

relations.note: Euler trails are graph-theoretic walks characterized by edge use and vertex-degree parity rather than geometric distances.

record.card: Transit photometry looks for repeated dips in starlight when a planet crosses its star from our viewpoint. The interval between dips gives the orbital period. Combined with the star’s mass, that timing constrains orbit size, but only suitably aligned systems produce transits.

evidence.locator: Transits: Planets Found in Dips in Light
evidence.note: Brightness dips, period and stellar-mass dependence of inferred orbit size.

record.label: Exoplanet transit photometry
record.learning_takeaway: Use recurring stellar dimming to detect planets and infer orbital information when geometry aligns.

relations.note: The detection method measures the brightness loss during an astronomical transit and uses repeated crossings to infer an orbit.

record.card: Robert Nozick’s experience machine imagines a device that supplies a lifetime of desired experiences without the corresponding real achievements. Would plugging in provide everything that makes life good? The thought experiment challenges experience-only accounts of well-being, but disagreement about our intuitions keeps the argument open.

evidence.note: The imagined device, real achievement contrast, and caution about treating the objection as decisive are explicit.

record.label: Experience machine
record.learning_takeaway: Test whether simulated desirable experience would provide everything that makes a life go well.

relations.note: The thought experiment tests what constitutes a good life and therefore connects to ethical evaluation of well-being.

record.card: Scotland’s Falkirk Wheel lifts canal boats in opposed water-filled chambers. A floating boat displaces water equal to its own weight, so admitting boats need not change each chamber’s total weight. That balance lets the wheel rotate while using comparatively little power.

evidence.note: Floating displacement maintains chamber weight and balances rotation.

record.label: Falkirk Wheel
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why floating boats can enter the wheel’s caissons without upsetting their weight balance.

relations.note: The wheel’s balancing mechanism explicitly applies Archimedes’ principle: entering boats replace their weight in water in the caissons.

record.card: Wood contains water in cell cavities and within cell walls. The fiber saturation point describes walls saturated with bound water after free cavity water is gone. Below this approximate boundary, losing wall-bound water changes dimensions; its measured value varies with wood and method.

evidence.locator: Fiber Saturation, pp. 4–2 to 4–3; Dimensional Stability, p. 4–7
evidence.note: The fiber-saturation discussion defines bound versus free water, identifies dimensional change below the boundary, and qualifies specimen/method variation.

record.label: Fiber saturation point in wood
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water bound in cell walls from free cavity water and locate the practical onset of moisture-sensitive wood properties.

relations.note: The fiber-saturation boundary concerns water in wood cell walls versus cavities and marks a practical change in moisture-dependent properties.

record.card: An obsidian tool can survive a fire while losing useful dating evidence. Heating may alter its surface enough to invalidate obsidian hydration dating. The problem separates two kinds of preservation: a recognizable artifact can remain even after the surface information needed for dating has changed.

evidence.locator: Wildfire impacts, paragraph beginning Wildland fires can impact archeological resources
evidence.note: Wildfire heat can alter a surface so hydration dating is unusable.

record.label: Fire alteration of obsidian hydration evidence
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize that heating can invalidate a dating surface without requiring complete artifact destruction.

relations.note: Fire-related surface alteration is a documented limitation on using obsidian hydration to infer an artifact’s age.

record.card: Under FIDE’s 2023 laws, five appearances of the same chess position end the game in a draw without a player’s claim. Identical piece placement alone is insufficient: the player to move and available moves must also match, including relevant castling and en passant rights.

evidence.note: Defines position identity and the automatic five-occurrence draw; commentary explicitly requires arbiter intervention.

record.label: Fivefold repetition in chess
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish an automatic repetition draw from a player’s threefold-repetition claim.

relations.note: The drawn-game articles specify this chess termination condition and define which positions count as repetitions.

record.card: In Gérard Genette’s framework, focalization concerns which information a narrative makes available. A story may restrict itself to one character’s knowledge even when someone else narrates. Separating access to information from the identity of the speaker makes narrative viewpoint more precise than a first-person/third-person label.

evidence.locator: Definition; Explication, paragraphs on knowledge restrictions and voice
evidence.note: Information restriction; distinction between focalization and narrator/voice.

record.label: Focalization
record.learning_takeaway: Separate restrictions on narrative information from the identity of the speaker.

relations.note: Focalization gives literary criticism a way to analyze information limits separately from the narrator’s identity.

record.card: A morpheme is a small unit pairing form with meaning. Some, such as cook, can stand alone; others, such as the past-tense -ed in cooked, must attach to another form. This free–bound distinction explains why meaningful pieces need not be independent words.

evidence.locator: Video Script: free and bound morphemes; cooked and carrots
evidence.note: Morpheme definition; free occurrence versus required attachment; cooked.

record.label: Free and bound morphemes
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish meaning-bearing units that stand alone from those requiring attachment.

relations.note: Morphological analysis distinguishes units that can occur alone from units whose distribution requires attachment.

record.card: Free indirect discourse can retain a narrator’s third-person pronouns and past tense while borrowing a character’s expressions, judgments, or sense of “now.” The result blends voices without a clear “she thought” frame. Context often matters more than a single grammatical marker for recognizing the technique.

evidence.note: Mixed person/tense and expressive cues; absence of frame; contextual recognition.

record.label: Free indirect discourse
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize the blend of narratorial grammar and a character’s expressions or viewpoint.

relations.note: The technique offers literary critics a specific way to track interaction between narratorial wording and a character’s thought or speech.

record.card: Freezing-point depression lets a solution stay liquid below its pure solvent’s freezing temperature. For dilute ideal solutions, the shift depends on solute-particle concentration. Spreading salt on icy roads uses this effect; seawater can likewise remain liquid below the freezing point of fresh water.

evidence.locator: Freezing Point Depression, opening definition and deicing examples
evidence.note: Dilute-solution shift, deicing and seawater examples.

record.label: Freezing-point depression
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why dilute solutions freeze below the pure solvent’s freezing point and why particle concentration matters.

relations.note: Dissolved particles alter a solution’s freezing temperature; this is a composition-dependent property beyond the definition of a homogeneous mixture.

record.card: The geoid models the sea surface after removing tides and currents, extended mathematically through the continents. Its gentle irregularities reflect Earth’s uneven gravitational field. Surveyors use this reference surface when determining elevations, so “height above sea level” involves a physical model rather than a perfectly smooth globe.

evidence.locator: Main explanation of idealized sea surface and elevations
evidence.note: Idealized sea surface, gravity variations, continental extension and elevations.

record.label: Geoid
record.learning_takeaway: Understand the idealized gravity-shaped sea surface used as a reference for elevation.

relations.note: Geodesy uses gravity observations and the geoid model to supply a physical reference for measuring elevations.

record.card: Git stores data as objects addressed by hashes of their contents plus a header. The object’s identifier is a retrieval key, not a filename. This separates the question of which data is stored from what a working file happens to be called.

evidence.locator: Git Objects, hash-object explanation and hash input
evidence.note: Content-derived retrieval keys include object header and data.

record.label: Git content-addressed object storage
record.learning_takeaway: Use content-derived identifiers to retrieve Git objects while distinguishing object content from a working-file name.

relations.note: Editorial implementation bridge: Git’s content-addressed object mechanism supports storing and retrieving data for the broader practice of version control.

record.card: A foreground star’s gravity can briefly magnify the light of a more distant star. A planet accompanying the lensing star may add a smaller disturbance to that brightening. Gravitational microlensing therefore finds worlds by their effect on another star’s light.

evidence.note: Foreground lens amplification and additional planetary perturbation.

record.label: Gravitational microlensing
record.learning_takeaway: Understand temporary magnification from foreground gravity and how a planet can perturb the brightening.

relations.note: Editorial placement in astronomy: an alignment-driven magnification of background starlight becomes evidence about a foreground planetary system.

record.card: A gravity assist bends a spacecraft’s path around a moving planet. In an ideal unpowered encounter, its distant incoming and outgoing speeds relative to that planet match, yet its speed relative to the Sun can change as momentum is exchanged.

evidence.locator: How It Works, planet-relative vectors and momentum exchange
evidence.note: Frame-dependent speed change in idealized flyby.

record.label: Gravity assist
record.learning_takeaway: Separate planet-relative trajectory bending from a spacecraft’s gain or loss of Sun-relative momentum.

relations.note: Editorial placement in celestial mechanics: mutual gravitation bends an orbital trajectory and transfers momentum between spacecraft and planet.

record.card: Dew-like drops along a leaf’s edges can come from inside the plant. When transpiration is low, osmotic root pressure can push liquid through outlets called hydathodes. This process, guttation, releases water containing small amounts of dissolved minerals and sugars.

evidence.locator: Opening explanation and root-pressure mechanism, lines 40–51
evidence.note: The article explains osmotic root pressure, low-transpiration conditions, hydathode outlets, and minerals/sugars in exuded liquid.

record.label: Guttation
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish root-pressure-driven liquid droplets at leaf edges from atmospheric dew.

relations.note: Editorial placement: this plant-water phenomenon links root osmotic pressure to specialized liquid outlets at leaf margins.

record.card: Hall’s marriage theorem tests whether one side of a finite bipartite graph can receive distinct partners. Every subset on that side must collectively have at least as many neighboring vertices as members. Surprisingly, this necessary condition is also sufficient for a matching.

evidence.note: Finite bipartite matching of one side and all-subsets neighbor condition.

record.label: Hall’s marriage theorem
record.learning_takeaway: Recognize that every subset needing matches must collectively have enough distinct neighbors, a sufficient as well as necessary condition.

relations.note: The theorem determines existence of a graph matching by comparing each subset of one vertex part with its neighbor set.

record.card: A Harris matrix diagrams the relative order of archaeological deposits and surfaces. A single section through a site cannot necessarily show all their relationships. Combining records into a matrix helps reconstruct how a complex site developed through time, beyond what physical depth alone can establish.

evidence.locator: The Harris Matrix and Its Significance to Archaeology; Changing the Stratigraphic Paradigm
evidence.note: Stratigraphic units, surfaces, relative sequence and limitations of sections.

record.label: Harris matrix
record.learning_takeaway: Represent relative stratigraphic relationships that one excavation profile cannot capture.

relations.note: The matrix organizes excavated units and surfaces into a relative sequence for reconstructing an archaeological site’s development.

record.card: An HTTP method is idempotent when repeating an identical request has the same intended server effect as sending it once. Responses can still differ. This property allows certain interrupted requests, such as PUT, to be retried without multiplying the intended change.

evidence.note: Intended-effect definition, differing responses and retry rationale.

record.label: HTTP method idempotency
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish repeated intended effects from identical responses or an absence of side effects.

relations.note: Editorial Web-protocol placement: this HTTP semantic rule determines how clients can repeat state-changing requests after uncertain communication outcomes.

record.card: An HTTP If-Match header can make an update depend on a previously observed entity tag. The server uses a strong comparison before applying the operation. If another writer has changed that representation, a mismatching tag prevents an accidental overwrite of the intervening work.

evidence.locator: §13.1.1 If-Match, strong comparison and lost-update explanation
evidence.note: Representation validator precondition and overwrite prevention.

record.label: HTTP If-Match update preconditions
record.learning_takeaway: Condition a state-changing request on a matching representation tag to avoid overwriting an intervening change.

relations.note: Editorial Web-protocol placement: the HTTP precondition provides optimistic coordination for competing writers by checking current representation identity before mutation.

record.card: Implementation intentions connect a specific cue to a planned response: if a chosen situation occurs, then a particular action follows. Unlike merely wanting an outcome, this plan spells out when and how to begin. Its usefulness depends partly on choosing a workable cue and an effective response.

evidence.locator: Overview; pp.6–7; Precision and Selecting an Effective Response, pp.9–12
evidence.note: If–then structure, goal/implementation distinction, specificity, viability, and instrumentality support the card.

record.label: Implementation intentions
record.learning_takeaway: Turn a goal into a cue-linked action plan with a specified if–then contingency.

relations.note: Cue-linked plans apply psychological mechanisms of attention and action regulation to carrying out goals; psychology is the broader field for this behavior-change method.

record.card: Adding the sizes of overlapping finite sets counts shared members more than once. Inclusion–exclusion corrects this: subtract pairwise overlaps, then add triple overlaps back, continuing with alternating signs. For two sets, simply subtract their intersection from the sum of their sizes.

evidence.locator: Counting with Venn Diagrams; Principle of Inclusion/Exclusion
evidence.note: Overlap correction and the two-/three-set pattern.

record.label: Inclusion–exclusion principle
record.learning_takeaway: Correct double counting by subtracting intersections, with alternating corrections for more sets.

relations.note: Editorial combinatorics placement: the method counts a union by systematically correcting repeated membership in overlapping finite sets.

record.card: Inflection changes a word to express grammatical information such as number, tense, or case while retaining its core meaning and word class. Books adds plurality to book; sang marks past time for sing. Inflection can therefore involve an ending or a change inside the word.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: number, tense, agreement and case
evidence.note: Grammatical information, retained category, plural endings and vowel-changing past forms.

record.label: Inflection (linguistics)
record.learning_takeaway: Separate grammatical changes to a word from creation of a new lexical word.

relations.note: Inflection is the word-structure process that expresses grammatical distinctions such as number, tense and case.

record.card: Information asymmetry occurs when one side of a transaction knows more than the other. A used-car seller may know defects that a buyer cannot see. This differs from uncertainty that both parties share, and helps explain why inspections, warranties, and reputations matter.

evidence.locator: Opening definitions; Mechanisms to Reduce the Risk of Imperfect Information
evidence.note: Defines unequal information; used-car and warranty/reputation examples explain possible responses.

record.label: Information asymmetry
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish unequal information between trading parties from uncertainty shared by both.

relations.note: Unequal knowledge changes participation and quality assessment in exchange; this is a specific economic mechanism within the broader study of markets.

record.card: Ireland’s 2016–2018 Citizens’ Assembly combined expert information, public submissions, and discussion among selected citizens. Its procedures encouraged roundtable questioning and used secret ballots when voting was required. This particular assembly shows how learning, deliberation, and a formal decision procedure can be organized together.

evidence.note: The dated body and its documented evidence, presentations, roundtable discussion, and secret voting procedures establish the case.

record.label: Irish Citizens’ Assembly (2016–2018)
record.learning_takeaway: Connect expert evidence, facilitated discussion, and secret ballots in a particular national assembly.

relations.note: This is the named Irish implementation of a citizens’ assembly, with specified learning, discussion, and voting procedures.

record.card: In the circular-orbit approximation, five Lagrange points let a small object keep pace with two massive orbiting bodies. The three collinear points are unstable. Triangular L4 and L5 can be stable when the larger bodies’ mass ratio is sufficiently unequal.

evidence.locator: Lagrange Points definition; stability and mass-ratio paragraphs
evidence.note: Five co-orbiting positions and conditional stability.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 1–2: restricted three-body model and fixed-separation rotating frame; pp. 7–8: L4/L5 stability
evidence.note: Restricted small-third-mass model with constant separation and angular rate; conditional linear stability of triangular points.

record.label: Lagrange points
record.learning_takeaway: Identify five co-orbiting equilibrium positions and distinguish unstable collinear points from conditionally stable triangular points.

relations.note: Editorial placement in celestial mechanics: the locations solve a restricted orbital-gravity balance for a small mass moving with two larger bodies.
Editorial navigation: the existing halo-orbit description concerns paths near L1–L3; equilibrium locations and nearby trajectories are distinct orbital subjects.

record.card: A lahar is a fast-moving mixture of water, mud, and volcanic rock flowing down a volcano’s drainage channels. Eruptions can create one by melting snow, but heavy rain or sudden water releases can also trigger flows while a volcano is not erupting.

evidence.note: The USGS summary defines the water/mud/volcanic-rock flow and lists snowmelt, rain and water releases as triggers, including inactive periods.

record.label: Lahar
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water-rich volcanic debris flows from lava and recognize that an eruption is not required.

relations.note: Lahars transport volcanic debris and water through a volcano’s drainage network and may be triggered without an eruption.

record.card: The Landscape Evolution Observatory at Biosphere 2 uses three replicated artificial hillslopes filled with crushed basalt. Dense sensor networks follow water, carbon, and energy flows as the landscapes develop. Controlled rainfall and climate allow researchers to test interactions that are difficult to isolate outdoors.

evidence.note: The official description specifies three replicated crushed-basalt slopes, extensive sensors and climate/rainfall control for coupled landscape research.

record.label: Landscape Evolution Observatory
record.learning_takeaway: See why replicated artificial hillslopes let researchers measure coupled soil, water and biological changes under controlled conditions.

relations.note: LEO is an Earth-science experiment whose controlled replicated hillslopes measure coupled water, substrate and biological changes.

record.card: Langar is the communal meal offered to everyone at a Sikh gurdwara. Sharing food and sitting at the same level express human equality across social divisions. The meal is vegetarian to make sharing easier across religious lines; that does not mean all Sikhs are themselves vegetarian.

evidence.locator: Summary; communal equality and vegetarian meal paragraphs
evidence.note: Open communal meal, equal seating, equality, and reason for vegetarian food.

record.label: Langar
record.learning_takeaway: Relate common food and equal seating to Sikh commitments to human equality.

relations.note: Langar puts Sikh commitments to equality and hospitality into practice through a shared meal open to visitors.

record.card: A finite wing pays an aerodynamic cost for making lift. Flow around its tips forms vortices that alter the surrounding airflow and tilt part of the aerodynamic force rearward. This lift-induced drag depends on lift and wing geometry, including aspect ratio.

evidence.locator: Air Pressure of a Wing; Drag Coefficient
evidence.note: Vortex-induced rearward force and dependence on lift and geometry.

record.label: Lift-induced drag
record.learning_takeaway: Explain why producing lift on a finite wing also creates a rearward aerodynamic force.

relations.note: Induced drag is explicitly an aerodynamic force component arising from the three-dimensional airflow of a finite lifting wing.

record.card: A light echo occurs when a flash reaches surrounding dust and scattered light arrives after the direct flash. Around V838 Monocerotis, changing illumination looked like expanding debris, even though it was revealing material already present. The apparent expansion traced light’s journey.

evidence.locator: Expanding Light Echo of V838 Monocerotis; reflected-light explanation
evidence.note: Finite light travel, reflection by existing dust and apparent expansion.

record.label: Light echo
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish delayed illumination of pre-existing dust from an expanding shell of newly ejected matter.

relations.note: Editorial placement under light: delayed scattering along longer paths produces changing illumination without requiring dust to move with the visible pattern.

record.card: Lithography prints from a flat surface rather than carved relief or grooves. A greasy drawing on prepared stone or metal attracts ink, while damp non-image areas repel it. The resulting separation lets a drawing’s marks transfer to paper without making its outlines into physical cuts.

evidence.note: Flat prepared matrix; greasy ink-receptive areas and damp ink-repellent areas.

record.label: Lithography (printmaking)
record.learning_takeaway: Separate a flat ink-selective printing surface from cut relief or incised processes.

relations.note: Lithography transfers an image using chemically differentiated areas of a flat printing matrix.

record.card: Charles Cooley’s looking-glass self describes how self-understanding develops through imagined reactions from other people. We picture how we appear, interpret others’ responses, and form judgments about ourselves. The “mirror” is our interpretation of their viewpoint, so it need not accurately reveal what they actually think.

evidence.note: Cooley’s theory explicitly uses imagined appearance, inferred reactions, and resulting self-understanding.

record.label: Looking-glass self
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how imagined judgments by other people feed into self-understanding.

relations.note: The social-interaction account explains formation of a sense of self through perceived appraisals, within the sociology chapter’s presentation-of-self discussion.

record.card: A compass follows the local magnetic field, which need not align with true north. The angle between those directions is magnetic declination. Because it changes with both location and time, converting a compass direction to true north requires a correction appropriate to where and when you measure.

evidence.locator: Magnetic Declination; FAQ on compass direction
evidence.note: Local field direction; angle from true north; location/time dependence.

record.label: Magnetic declination
record.learning_takeaway: Account for the changing angle between local magnetic north and true north.

relations.note: Declination is the directional correction needed when navigation combines magnetic-compass observations with true-north bearings.

record.card: Mean ceramic dating uses a group of pottery fragments to estimate a site’s occupation period. Known production dates of ceramic types are combined across the assemblage. The resulting average concerns the collection’s chronology; it does not establish the exact burial date of every sherd.

evidence.locator: Ceramic assemblage and mean ceramic date paragraphs
evidence.note: Ceramic production dates and assemblage mean as occupation estimate.

record.label: Mean ceramic dating
record.learning_takeaway: Estimate occupation from a ceramic assemblage rather than dating a deposit by one object.

relations.note: Historical archaeologists combine ceramic production chronologies to estimate the occupation represented by an assemblage.

record.card: Melodic inversion reverses the direction of a tune’s intervals, turning upward motion downward and vice versa. A real inversion preserves exact interval qualities; a tonal inversion adjusts them to stay within a key. The distinction explains how a recognizable mirrored shape can retain different pitch details.

evidence.note: Defines inversion and distinguishes real interval-quality preservation from tonal adaptation to scale or key.

record.label: Melodic inversion
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish reversing melodic interval direction from changing note order.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents inversion as one method of altering a melody while relating it to its original motive.

record.card: Mezzotint begins with a roughened metal plate that would print dark all over. The artist scrapes and burnishes selected areas so they retain less ink and appear lighter. Instead of building shadows mainly from lines, the image develops through controlled transitions from dark to light.

evidence.note: Roughened dark ground; scraping and burnishing create lighter tones.

record.label: Mezzotint
record.learning_takeaway: Build light areas by smoothing an initially ink-holding roughened plate.

relations.note: Mezzotint makes an intaglio image by selectively smoothing an initially rough, ink-holding metal surface.

record.card: A mihrab is a niche indicating the direction of Mecca in a mosque or religious school. It gives prayer an architectural focus and can also carry elaborate ornament. The Met’s fourteenth-century Iranian example combines a recessed niche with cut-tile mosaics and religious inscriptions.

evidence.note: Prayer-direction niche; fourteenth-century Iranian tilework and inscriptions.

record.label: Mihrab
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a prayer-direction niche from the direction it indicates, and see its ornamental role.

relations.note: The niche organizes sacred space around prayer direction while its ornament makes that directional focus visually prominent.

record.card: Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank in Sussex conserves wild plant seeds for research and restoration. Its laboratories study germination alongside long-term cold storage. The collection is therefore a living resource intended to help rebuild ecosystems, with stored seeds serving as a starting point for renewed growth.

evidence.note: The Kew description locates the wild-seed bank in Sussex and combines cold storage, germination research, and restoration use.

record.label: Millennium Seed Bank
record.learning_takeaway: Understand how conserved wild seeds supply research and ecosystem restoration beyond storage.

relations.note: Kew stores and studies wild seeds so they can support research and habitat restoration, an explicit plant-conservation purpose.

record.card: Fan and van differ in just one speech sound and have different meanings in English. Such a minimal pair is evidence that the two sounds belong to different phonemes, or sound categories. The comparison concerns pronunciation, so matching or differing spellings alone cannot establish it.

evidence.locator: Video Script: fan/van and minimal-pair diagnosis
evidence.note: English fan/van, phonemic contrast and pronunciation rather than spelling.

record.label: Minimal pair
record.learning_takeaway: Use a one-sound meaning contrast as evidence for separate phonemes.

relations.note: Comparing minimally different words is a phonological diagnostic for whether a sound difference distinguishes meaning.

record.card: Molality counts moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Unlike molarity, which uses solution volume, its denominator does not expand as temperature rises. That makes molality useful when calculating temperature-dependent changes such as freezing-point depression without changing the concentration scale.

evidence.locator: Mole Fraction and Molality; Freezing Point Depression equation
evidence.note: Mass-based concentration and temperature independence.

record.label: Molality
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish moles per kilogram of solvent from volume-based molarity and understand temperature independence.

relations.note: Molality is one concentration measure, using solvent mass rather than the volume denominator of molarity.

record.card: A monotonic clock is useful for measuring elapsed time because its readings do not jump backward when the system’s civil clock is adjusted. Python’s monotonic clock has an unspecified starting point: differences between readings are meaningful, but an isolated value is not a calendar timestamp.

evidence.note: Nondecreasing timing, independence from system clock updates and undefined reference point.

record.label: Monotonic clocks for elapsed time
record.learning_takeaway: Distinguish duration measurement from civil time using a clock unaffected by wall-clock jumps.

relations.note: Editorial programming placement: duration measurement must use a clock whose ordering survives civil-time adjustments, a concrete API design concern.

record.card: Moral hazard arises when protection from a loss changes incentives to avoid it. An insured business might invest less in theft prevention because an insurer bears part of the cost. Deductibles leave some losses with the policyholder, potentially preserving incentives for care.

evidence.note: Business security example and deductibles show changed incentives under coverage.

record.label: Moral hazard
record.learning_takeaway: Explain how protection from consequences can change behavior after an agreement.

relations.note: The shift in incentives when another party bears costs is an economic problem of behavior under a contract; insurance supplies the documented example.

record.card: Moral luck asks how events outside someone’s control can affect moral judgment. Two equally careless drivers might both suffer brake failure, yet only one encounters a person in the road. Judging them differently creates tension with the principle that blame should track what an agent controls.

evidence.note: The source contrasts the control principle with differently assessed negligent drivers and outcomes.

record.label: Moral luck
record.learning_takeaway: Examine tension between judging people only for what they control and judging different outcomes differently.
